title: Priority Task Board
statement:
Build a task board shared by several people. Every task has an owner, a unique taskId and a priority.

  • TaskBoard(tasks) starts the board with a list of [owner, taskId, priority] triples.
  • add(owner, taskId, priority) puts a new task on the board. taskId is not on the board at that moment (it may have been used earlier and removed).
  • edit(taskId, newPriority) changes the priority of a task that is on the board.
  • remove(taskId) takes a task that is on the board off it.
  • runTop() takes the task with the highest priority off the board and returns its owner. If several tasks share that priority, the one with the largest taskId goes first. Return -1 if the board is empty.

Every call should take O(log n) time on average. Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the board. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: Tasks 20 and 30 tie at priority 8, so the larger id 30 runs first. Task 20 is then lowered to 2 and only runs after 40; task 10 was removed, so the board ends empty.
Task 1 no longer has priority 9 after the edit, so task 2 (priority 5) runs before it.
Id 5 was removed and then added again by owner 9. Nothing about the old task 5 may leak into the answer.

constraints: At most 100 000 calls after the constructor
hints: A map from taskId to its owner and current priority handles add, edit and remove. What makes runTop fast?
A max-heap ordered by (priority, taskId) gives the top task. But a heap cannot cheaply find and change an entry in the middle.
Do not change heap entries. On edit push a new entry; on remove do nothing to the heap. In runTop, pop entries until the top one still matches the map (the task exists and has that priority).

explain.intuition:
The map is the source of truth: for each task on the board it stores the owner and the current priority. The heap is only an index for "which task is on top", and it is allowed to hold outdated entries. That is lazy deletion. An edit just pushes a fresh (priority, taskId) pair; a removal only deletes from the map.

When runTop looks at the heap's top, it checks the entry against the map. If the task is gone, or its current priority differs, the entry is stale: pop it and look again. Each pushed entry is popped at most once, so the total work stays O(log n) per call on average. A UI job queue that marks cancelled jobs and skips them when they reach the front works the same way.
steps: Keep info: taskId → (owner, priority) and a max-heap of (priority, taskId), ties broken by the larger id.
add: store the task in the map and push its pair. edit: update the priority in the map and push the new pair.
remove: delete the task from the map only.

runTop: while the heap's top is stale (task missing from the map, or priority in the map differs), pop it. If the heap is empty return -1; otherwise pop the top, delete its task from the map and return the owner.
pitfalls: Checking only that the task id exists. After an edit the old entry still points to an existing task, with the wrong priority, as in the second example.
Storing the owner inside heap entries and returning it. When an id is removed and added again by a new owner, an old entry can report the wrong owner, as in the third example.
Breaking priority ties by the smaller task id. The rule here is the larger id first.

solutions.title: Map plus a full scan on runTop
solutions.idea: Keep only the map. runTop scans every task to find the best one.
solutions.time: O(1) for add, edit, remove; O(n) for runTop

solutions.title: Heap with lazy deletion
solutions.idea: Push a new heap entry on every add and edit; never search the heap. runTop discards entries that no longer match the map.

followups: Many edits pile up stale entries. When would you rebuild the heap from the map, and what does that cost?
Add peekOwner(owner): the top task of one particular owner, also in O(log n).
